Ordinarily,
a plaint in a suit for maintenance falls under section 7(i) and (ii), Court
Fees Act and attracts ad valorem courtâ€‘fee on the amount claimed to be
computed in accordance with Article 1, Schedule I of the Court Fees Act. But,
section 19 of the West Pakistan Family Courts Act, 1964 alters the law in this
respect and enacts that notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in
the Court Fees Act, 1870, the courtâ€‘fee to be paid on any plaint filed
before a Family Court shall be Re. 1. The concession with regard to reduction
in the courtâ€‘fee is restricted to a 'plaint'. The omission of 'memorandum
of appeal' in this section is significant, particularly, as both a plaint and a
memorandum of appeal are included in Article 1, Schedule I of the Court Fees
Act, as attracting ad valorem courtâ€‘fees. On the principle of expression
'unius est exclusio alterius' (the express mention of one implies the exclusion
of the other), it is clear that the Legislature intended to exclude from the
purview of section 19 of the said Act, the 'memorandum of appeal'. The
concession with regard to payment of courtâ€‘fees on a 'plaint' filed
before a Family Court, which has been granted to a petitioner, who is generally
a married woman, seeking to enforce her family rights, is not to apply to a
memorandum of appeal.

Hasan Asghar
Rizvi for Petitioner.

ORDER

I.MAHMOOD,J.
â€‘â€‘ Petitioner Mst. Hameeda Begum, filed a Family Suit against
respondent No. 2, Ghulam Hyder for past and future maintenance. As the suit was
decreed for Rs.1,500 only, the petitioner filed an appeal to the District Court
and affixed a courtâ€‘fee of the value of Re. 1 only on the memo. of
appeal. During the pendency of the appeal the respondent No.2, moved an
application for the rejection of the memo. of appeal on the ground that the
petitioner/ appellant had failed to pay ad valorem courtâ€‘fee, as required
under section 7(1) of the Court Fees Act, 1870. The learned Additional District
Judge relying on the decision reported in Mohammad Anwar Khan v. Additional
District Judge, Rawalpindi PLD 1978 Lah. 716 held that the Memorandum of Appeal
arising out of a suit for maintenance attracted ad valorem courtâ€‘fee
under Article 1, Schedule I of the Court Fees Act, 1870. He, therefore,
dismissed the appeal.

2. Mr. Syed
Hassan Asghar Rizvi, learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that an
appeal is a continuation of a suit and unless there are specific provisions for
payment of different courtâ€‘fees, the courtâ€‘fees paid on the suit
was payable on the appeal also. We find no force in this submission.
Ordinarily, a plaint in a suit for maintenance falls under section 7(i) and
(ii), Court Fees Act and attracts ad valorem courtâ€‘fee on the amount
claimed to be computed in accordance with Article 1, Schedule I of the Court
Fees Act. But, section 19 of the West Pakistan Family Courts Act, 1964 alters
the law in this respect and enacts that notwithstanding anything to the
contrary contained in the Court Fees Act, 1870, the courtâ€‘fee to be paid
on any plaint filed before a Family Court shall be Re. 1. The concession with
regard to reduction in the courtâ€‘fee is restricted to a 'plaint'. The
omission of 'memorandum of appeal' in this section is significant,
particularly, as both a plaint and a memorandum of appeal are included in
Article 1, Schedule I of the Court Fees Act, as attracting ad valorem courtâ€‘fees.
On the principle of expression 'unius est exclusio alterius' (the express
mention of one implies the exclusion of the other), it is clear that the
Legislature intended to exclude from the purview of section 19 of the said Act,
the 'memorandum of appeal'. The concession with regard to payment of courtâ€‘fees
on a 'plaint' filed before a Family Court, which has been granted to a
petitioner, who is generally a married woman, seeking to enforce her family
rights, is not to apply to a memorandum of appeal.

3. The next
submission of Mr. S.H. Rizvi is that a Family Court is not a Civil Court, and
therefore, according to him, section 6 of the Court Fees Act, which prohibits
the receiving of a memorandum of appeal unless the courtâ€‘fee indicated in
the Schedule has been paid on the document, does not apply. This argument was
fully considered by the Lahore High Court in Muhammad Anwar Khan v. Additional
District Judge, Rawalpindi P L D 1978 Lah. 716 and was repelled. We are in
respectful agreement with the reasoning of that judgment. The Family Court is a
Civil Court, despite the exclusion of the Civil Procedure Code and the Evidence
Act in their application to proceedings before the Family Court. Moreover, the
appeal in question was filed before the District Court under section 14 of the
West Pakistan Family Courts Act. The District Court is undoubtedly, a Civil
Court. There can be no doubt, therefore, that a memorandum of appeal to be
filed before the District Court falls under Article 1 of Schedule I of the
Court Fees Act, and courtâ€‘fee in such cases is payable ad valorem on the
subjectâ€‘matter in dispute.

4. For
these reasons, we find no force in this petition, which is accordingly,
summarily dismissed.
